L07 · Singular Value Decomposition

L07 · Singular Value Decomposition

Lecture 7 (slides "Singular Value Decomposition", 20 pages) · Deisenroth §3.2.3 and Ch. 4 · Strang Ch. 7

Lecture 7 slides (PDF) Revision notes: SVD via a flat-to-3D filter Problem Set 7 with solutions (P1–P4, P9, P11 are SVD) Read them all on this page ↓

The eigen-decomposition of L06 needs a square matrix, and it is only clean for symmetric ones. The singular value decomposition (SVD) works for every matrix. In order, this lecture covers: positive and negative (semi-)definite matrices, with their geometric meaning and the eigenvalue test; the SVD A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤, its shapes and its vocabulary; how to compute it from A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤; its geometric meaning (rotate, stretch, rotate: a circle becomes an ellipse); the rank of a matrix and rank estimation from noisy data; and low-rank matrix approximation.

Intuition: The flat-to-3D filter (revision notes)

A graphics program lifts a flat picture onto a tilted sheet in 3D: a pixel x∈R2x\in\mathbb{R}^2x∈R2 goes to Ax∈R3Ax\in\mathbb{R}^3Ax∈R3 with
A=[1−0.80110]∈R3×2.A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-0.8\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times2}.A=​101​−0.810​​∈R3×2.
A round logo of radius 1 becomes a tilted oval lying on one flat sheet inside R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 (every output satisfies y3=y1+0.8 y2y_3=y_1+0.8\,y_2y3​=y1​+0.8y2​).

We would like the "eigen" description of L06 — directions that AAA only stretches. But Aq=λqAq=\lambda qAq=λq is impossible here: q∈R2q\in\mathbb{R}^2q∈R2 while Aq∈R3Aq\in\mathbb{R}^3Aq∈R3. The SVD fixes this by allowing different special directions on the input side (vi∈R2v_i\in\mathbb{R}^2vi​∈R2) and on the output side (ui∈R3u_i\in\mathbb{R}^3ui​∈R3):
Avi=σiui.Av_i=\sigma_iu_i .Avi​=σi​ui​.

#1. Positive and negative definite matrices

🧩Background you needthe quadratic form x⊤Axx^\top Axx⊤Ax, and what a dot product's sign means

A 1×n1\times n1×n row times an n×nn\times nn×n matrix times an n×1n\times1n×1 column is a single number

For A=[2112]A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}A=[21​12​] and x=[x1x2]x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}x=[x1​x2​​]:
Ax=[2x1+x2x1+2x2],x⊤Ax=[x1x2][2x1+x2x1+2x2]=2x12+2x1x2+2x22.Ax=\begin{bmatrix}2x_1+x_2\\x_1+2x_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad x^\top Ax=\begin{bmatrix}x_1&x_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2x_1+x_2\\x_1+2x_2\end{bmatrix}=2x_1^2+2x_1x_2+2x_2^2 .Ax=[2x1​+x2​x1​+2x2​​],x⊤Ax=[x1​​x2​​][2x1​+x2​x1​+2x2​​]=2x12​+2x1​x2​+2x22​.
Every term has degree 2 in the entries of xxx — that is why it is called a quadratic form.

The sign of a dot product is the sign of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ

From L01, u⊤w=∥u∥ ∥w∥cos⁡θu^\top w=\|u\|\,\|w\|\cos\thetau⊤w=∥u∥∥w∥cosθ. The lengths are positive, so
u⊤w>0  ⟺  θ<90∘,u⊤w=0  ⟺  θ=90∘,u⊤w<0  ⟺  θ>90∘.u^\top w>0\iff\theta<90^\circ,\qquad u^\top w=0\iff\theta=90^\circ,\qquad u^\top w<0\iff\theta>90^\circ .u⊤w>0⟺θ<90∘,u⊤w=0⟺θ=90∘,u⊤w<0⟺θ>90∘.
Since x⊤Ax=x⋅(Ax)x^\top Ax=x\cdot(Ax)x⊤Ax=x⋅(Ax) is the dot product of xxx with its own image, its sign says whether AAA keeps xxx pointing "forwards" or turns it "backwards".

Definition: Definite and semi-definite matrices

For A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n:
x⊤Ax≥0  for all x∈Rn⟹ A is positive semi-definite (PSD), written A⪰0,x⊤Ax>0  for all x≠0⟹ A is positive definite (PD), written A≻0,x⊤Ax≤0  for all x⟹ A is negative semi-definite (NSD),x⊤Ax<0  for all x≠0⟹ A is negative definite (ND).\begin{aligned} x^\top Ax&\ge0\ \ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n &&\Longrightarrow\ A\text{ is \textbf{positive semi-definite} (PSD), written }A\succeq0,\\ x^\top Ax&>0\ \ \text{for all }x\neq\mathbf 0 &&\Longrightarrow\ A\text{ is \textbf{positive definite} (PD), written }A\succ0,\\ x^\top Ax&\le0\ \ \text{for all }x &&\Longrightarrow\ A\text{ is \textbf{negative semi-definite} (NSD)},\\ x^\top Ax&<0\ \ \text{for all }x\neq\mathbf 0 &&\Longrightarrow\ A\text{ is \textbf{negative definite} (ND)}. \end{aligned}x⊤Axx⊤Axx⊤Axx⊤Ax​≥0  for all x∈Rn>0  for all x=0≤0  for all x<0  for all x=0​​⟹ A is positive semi-definite (PSD), written A⪰0,⟹ A is positive definite (PD), written A≻0,⟹ A is negative semi-definite (NSD),⟹ A is negative definite (ND).​
If x⊤Axx^\top Axx⊤Ax takes both signs, AAA is indefinite. (The strict versions must exclude x=0x=\mathbf 0x=0, since 0⊤A0=0\mathbf 0^\top A\mathbf 0=00⊤A0=0 for every matrix; the slide writes "∀x\forall x∀x" as shorthand.)

The interpretation (slides p4–5). Let y=Axy=Axy=Ax. Then x⊤Ax=x⊤yx^\top Ax=x^\top yx⊤Ax=x⊤y, and:

  • PSD: x⊤y≥0x^\top y\ge0x⊤y≥0, so the angle between xxx and AxAxAx is at most π/2\pi/2π/2. Graphically, AxAxAx can be anywhere in the half-plane on the side of xxx, including the dashed boundary line where x⊤Ax=0x^\top Ax=0x⊤Ax=0.
  • PD: x⊤y>0x^\top y>0x⊤y>0, so the angle is strictly less than π/2\pi/2π/2: the half-plane excluding the boundary.

A PSD matrix never turns a vector by more than a right angle; an indefinite matrix turns some vectors forwards and others backwards.

#The eigenvalue test (symmetric matrices)

Theorem / Key result: Eigenvalues decide the sign

For a symmetric AAA:
A≻0  ⟺  all λi>0,A⪰0  ⟺  all λi≥0,ND  ⟺  all λi<0,NSD  ⟺  all λi≤0,A\succ0\iff\text{all }\lambda_i>0,\qquad A\succeq0\iff\text{all }\lambda_i\ge0,\qquad \text{ND}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i<0,\qquad \text{NSD}\iff\text{all }\lambda_i\le0,A≻0⟺all λi​>0,A⪰0⟺all λi​≥0,ND⟺all λi​<0,NSD⟺all λi​≤0,
and AAA is indefinite if it has eigenvalues of both signs.

The slide's argument (one direction). The eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real (L06). If AAA is PD, take x=qx=qx=q, an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ:
q⊤Aq>0 ⟹ q⊤(λq)>0 ⟹ λ ∥q∥22>0 ⟹ λ>0.q^\top Aq>0\ \Longrightarrow\ q^\top(\lambda q)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\,\|q\|_2^2>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda>0 .q⊤Aq>0 ⟹ q⊤(λq)>0 ⟹ λ∥q∥22​>0 ⟹ λ>0.
In the same way, PSD gives λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0, NSD gives λ≤0\lambda\le0λ≤0 and ND gives λ<0\lambda<0λ<0.

🔍Where does this come from?the other direction: why positive eigenvalues force x⊤Ax>0x^\top Ax>0x⊤Ax>0 for every xxx

Write the symmetric matrix as A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ (L06) and describe xxx in the eigenvector basis, c=Q⊤xc=Q^\top xc=Q⊤x (so x=Qcx=Qcx=Qc). Then
x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=(Q⊤x)⊤Λ (Q⊤x)=c⊤Λc=[c1⋯cn][λ1⋱λn][c1⋮cn]=∑i=1nλi ci2.x^\top Ax=x^\top Q\Lambda Q^\top x=(Q^\top x)^\top\Lambda\,(Q^\top x)=c^\top\Lambda c =\begin{bmatrix}c_1&\cdots&c_n\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_1&&\\&\ddots&\\&&\lambda_n\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\\vdots\\c_n\end{bmatrix} =\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,c_i^2 .x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=(Q⊤x)⊤Λ(Q⊤x)=c⊤Λc=[c1​​⋯​cn​​]​λ1​​⋱​λn​​​​c1​⋮cn​​​=i=1∑n​λi​ci2​.
A sum of squares, each weighted by an eigenvalue. If every λi>0\lambda_i>0λi​>0 and x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0 (so c≠0c\neq\mathbf 0c=0, because QQQ is invertible), the sum is positive. If one λi\lambda_iλi​ is negative, choose c=eic=e_ic=ei​ (that is, x=qix=q_ix=qi​) to make the sum negative. So the signs of the eigenvalues decide everything.

Worked example: The three matrices of L06 (revision notes)
  1. S=[2112]S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}S=[21​12​] has λ=3,1\lambda=3,1λ=3,1, both positive: PD. Directly, x⊤Sx=2x12+2x1x2+2x22=x12+x22+(x1+x2)2>0x^\top Sx=2x_1^2+2x_1x_2+2x_2^2=x_1^2+x_2^2+(x_1+x_2)^2>0x⊤Sx=2x12​+2x1​x2​+2x22​=x12​+x22​+(x1​+x2​)2>0 for x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0.
  2. F=12[1111]F=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}F=21​[11​11​] has λ=1,0\lambda=1,0λ=1,0: PSD but not PD. Indeed x⊤Fx=12(x1+x2)2≥0x^\top Fx=\tfrac12(x_1+x_2)^2\ge0x⊤Fx=21​(x1​+x2​)2≥0, but it equals 000 at x=(1,−1)x=(1,-1)x=(1,−1), the eigenvector of λ=0\lambda=0λ=0.
  3. M=[3220]M=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\2&0\end{bmatrix}M=[32​20​] has λ=4,−1\lambda=4,-1λ=4,−1: indefinite. For x=(1,0)x=(1,0)x=(1,0), x⊤Mx=3>0x^\top Mx=3>0x⊤Mx=3>0; for x=(1,−2)x=(1,-2)x=(1,−2), Mx=(−1,2)Mx=(-1,2)Mx=(−1,2) and x⊤Mx=−1−4=−5<0x^\top Mx=-1-4=-5<0x⊤Mx=−1−4=−5<0.
  4. Check yourself: is [1221]\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{bmatrix}[12​21​] PD? Its trace is 222 and its determinant 1−4=−3<01-4=-3<01−4=−3<0, so the eigenvalues have opposite signs (333 and −1-1−1): indefinite, not PD.
Common trap: A positive determinant is not enough

det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0 only says the product of the eigenvalues is positive; two negative eigenvalues also give a positive product. −I-I−I has det⁡(−I)=1>0\det(-I)=1>0det(−I)=1>0 but is negative definite. (2024 Mid MCQ 22: "det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0" does not guarantee PSD; "all eigenvalues ≥0\ge0≥0", "x⊤Ax≥0x^\top Ax\ge0x⊤Ax≥0 for all xxx" and "A=B⊤BA=B^\top BA=B⊤B" all do.)

📄 Original question2024 Mid Part I · MCQ 22 ↗tap to show
  • 2024 MCQ 22. For symmetric AAA, which conditions guarantee that AAA is PSD? (a) all eigenvalues non-negative (b) x⊤Ax≥0x^\top Ax\ge0x⊤Ax≥0 for all xxx (c) A=B⊤BA=B^\top BA=B⊤B for some BBB (d) det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0

The level-curve picture (revision notes, Figure 3). The curves x⊤Ax=cx^\top Ax=cx⊤Ax=c are closed ellipses for a PD matrix (axes along the eigenvectors, half-lengths c/λi\sqrt{c/\lambda_i}c/λi​​), parallel lines for a PSD matrix with a zero eigenvalue (the ellipse stretched to infinity), and hyperbolas — a saddle — for an indefinite one.

Remember

PSD means x⊤Ax≥0x^\top Ax\ge0x⊤Ax≥0 for every xxx — AxAxAx never turns more than 90∘90^\circ90∘ from xxx — and for a symmetric matrix that is the same as all eigenvalues ≥0\ge0≥0 (PD: all >0>0>0).

#2. Gram matrices are always PSD

🧩Background you needwhy x⊤(A⊤A)x=∥Ax∥2x^\top(A^\top A)x=\|Ax\|^2x⊤(A⊤A)x=∥Ax∥2

Group the product differently and use (Ax)⊤=x⊤A⊤(Ax)^\top=x^\top A^\top(Ax)⊤=x⊤A⊤ (L02):
x⊤(A⊤A)x=(x⊤A⊤)(Ax)=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥22.x^\top(A^\top A)x=(x^\top A^\top)(Ax)=(Ax)^\top(Ax)=\|Ax\|_2^2 .x⊤(A⊤A)x=(x⊤A⊤)(Ax)=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥22​.
A squared length is never negative. This is the same step that proved the Gram matrix invertible in L02 (Tutorial 1).

📄 Original questionTutorial 1 · Question 1 ↗tap to show

Let AAA have linearly independent columns and G=A⊤AG=A^\top AG=A⊤A. Show that GGG is invertible, i.e. that Gx=0Gx=\mathbf 0Gx=0 forces x=0x=\mathbf 0x=0: left-multiply A⊤Ax=0A^\top Ax=\mathbf 0A⊤Ax=0 by x⊤x^\topx⊤, write x⊤A⊤Axx^\top A^\top Axx⊤A⊤Ax as (Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥2(Ax)^\top(Ax)=\|Ax\|^2(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥2, conclude Ax=0Ax=\mathbf 0Ax=0, and use the independence of the columns. (Full question and solution in the L02 notes.)

Take any A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, square or not. We cannot ask for its eigenvalues, but we can form two square, symmetric matrices, A⊤A∈Rn×nA^\top A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A⊤A∈Rn×n and AA⊤∈Rm×mAA^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}AA⊤∈Rm×m.

Theorem / Key result: A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are symmetric PSD

For every AAA,
x⊤(A⊤A)x=∥Ax∥2≥0andy⊤(AA⊤)y=∥A⊤y∥2≥0,x^\top(A^\top A)x=\|Ax\|^2\ge0\qquad\text{and}\qquad y^\top(AA^\top)y=\|A^\top y\|^2\ge0,x⊤(A⊤A)x=∥Ax∥2≥0andy⊤(AA⊤)y=∥A⊤y∥2≥0,
so both are PSD, their eigenvalues are real and ≥0\ge0≥0, and their square roots exist. Moreover, A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is PD exactly when the columns of AAA are independent (then Ax=0Ax=\mathbf 0Ax=0 only for x=0x=\mathbf 0x=0).

Meaning. The quadratic form of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is the squared length of the image: A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A knows how much AAA stretches each vector. That is the key to the SVD.

For the filter,
A⊤A=[101−0.810][1−0.80110]=[2−0.8−0.81.64]A^\top A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\-0.8&1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-0.8\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-0.8\\-0.8&1.64\end{bmatrix}A⊤A=[1−0.8​01​10​]​101​−0.810​​=[2−0.8​−0.81.64​]
is PD (the two columns of AAA are independent), while AA⊤∈R3×3AA^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}AA⊤∈R3×3 is only PSD: the sheet is flat, so one direction of R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 is never reached.

Check yourself. If A∈R5×3A\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times3}A∈R5×3 has rank 3, then A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A (3×33\times33×3, rank 3) is PD, and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ (5×55\times55×5, rank 3) has 5−3=25-3=25−3=2 zero eigenvalues.

Remember

A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are symmetric PSD for every matrix, because x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0x^\top A^\top Ax=\|Ax\|^2\ge0x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0; their eigenvalues are the squared stretch factors of AAA.

#3. The singular value decomposition

Overview (slide p9). The SVD is a central matrix decomposition. Strang (1993) called it the "fundamental theorem of linear algebra", because it applies to all matrices, not only square ones, and it always exists. For A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, the map x∈Rn↦Ax∈Rmx\in\mathbb{R}^n\mapsto Ax\in\mathbb{R}^mx∈Rn↦Ax∈Rm is a linear transformation, and the SVD explains its underlying geometry.

Theorem / Key result: Singular value decomposition

Every A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n can be written
A=U Σ V⊤,A=U\,\Sigma\,V^\top,A=UΣV⊤,
where

  • U∈Rm×mU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}U∈Rm×m is orthonormal (orthogonal): U⊤U=ImU^\top U=I_mU⊤U=Im​;
  • V∈Rn×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}V∈Rn×n is orthonormal: V⊤V=InV^\top V=I_nV⊤V=In​;
  • Σ∈Rm×n\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}Σ∈Rm×n is a (special) diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the singular values
    σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σmin⁡(m,n)≥0.\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_{\min(m,n)}\ge0 .σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σmin(m,n)​≥0.
    The columns uiu_iui​ of UUU are the left singular vectors (in the output space Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm); the columns viv_ivi​ of VVV are the right singular vectors (in the input space Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn).

The shape of Σ\SigmaΣ is the shape of AAA, so there are min⁡(m,n)\min(m,n)min(m,n) singular values:
[σ10⋯0⋱⋮⋮σm0⋯0]⏟m<n: extra zero columns[σ1⋱σn]⏟m=n[σ1⋱σn0⋯0⋮⋮0⋯0]⏟m>n: extra zero rows\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1&&&0&\cdots&0\\&\ddots&&\vdots&&\vdots\\&&\sigma_m&0&\cdots&0\end{bmatrix}}_{m<n:\ \text{extra zero columns}} \qquad \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1&&\\&\ddots&\\&&\sigma_n\end{bmatrix}}_{m=n} \qquad \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1&&\\&\ddots&\\&&\sigma_n\\0&\cdots&0\\\vdots&&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0\end{bmatrix}}_{m>n:\ \text{extra zero rows}}m<n: extra zero columns​σ1​​⋱​σm​​0⋮0​⋯⋯​0⋮0​​​​m=n​σ1​​⋱​σn​​​​​m>n: extra zero rows​σ1​0⋮0​⋱⋯⋯​σn​0⋮0​​​​

For the filter (m=3m=3m=3, n=2n=2n=2):
A⏟3×2=U⏟3×3 Σ⏟3×2 V⊤⏟2×2.\underbrace{A}_{3\times2}=\underbrace{U}_{3\times3}\,\underbrace{\Sigma}_{3\times2}\,\underbrace{V^\top}_{2\times2}.3×2A​​=3×3U​​3×2Σ​​2×2V⊤​​.
Always track the sizes: V⊤V^\topV⊤ acts on inputs in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, Σ\SigmaΣ converts Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn to Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm, and UUU acts on outputs in Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm.

#The one equation to remember

Multiply A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ on the right by VVV (and use V⊤V=IV^\top V=IV⊤V=I): AV=UΣAV=U\SigmaAV=UΣ. Reading this column by column,
Avi=σiuii=1,…,min⁡(m,n).\boxed{Av_i=\sigma_iu_i}\qquad i=1,\dots,\min(m,n).Avi​=σi​ui​​i=1,…,min(m,n).
AAA sends each right singular vector viv_ivi​ to the left singular vector uiu_iui​, stretched by σi\sigma_iσi​. Along the viv_ivi​, AAA does nothing but stretch (and move into the output space).

🔍Where does this come from?why AV=UΣAV=U\SigmaAV=UΣ reads column by column as Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​

Column iii of AVAVAV is AAA times column iii of VVV, i.e. AviAv_iAvi​ (L02: AB=[Ab1 ⋯ Abp]AB=[Ab_1\ \cdots\ Ab_p]AB=[Ab1​ ⋯ Abp​]). Column iii of UΣU\SigmaUΣ is UUU times column iii of Σ\SigmaΣ, which is σiei\sigma_ie_iσi​ei​ (one non-zero entry), so it equals σiUei=σiui\sigma_iUe_i=\sigma_iu_iσi​Uei​=σi​ui​. Equating column iii of both sides gives Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​.

Outer-product (compact) form. Multiplying out UΣV⊤U\Sigma V^\topUΣV⊤ one column at a time gives a sum of rank-one matrices (L02):
A=∑i=1min⁡(m,n)σi uivi⊤.A=\sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,n)}\sigma_i\,u_iv_i^\top .A=i=1∑min(m,n)​σi​ui​vi⊤​.
If only rrr singular values are non-zero, the remaining columns of UUU and VVV multiply zeros and can be dropped: A=UrΣrVr⊤A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\topA=Ur​Σr​Vr⊤​ with shapes (m×r)(r×r)(r×n)(m\times r)(r\times r)(r\times n)(m×r)(r×r)(r×n).

Check yourself. For A∈R5×3A\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times3}A∈R5×3: UUU is 5×55\times55×5, Σ\SigmaΣ is 5×35\times35×3, V⊤V^\topV⊤ is 3×33\times33×3; there are 3 singular values and the last 5−3=25-3=25−3=2 rows of Σ\SigmaΣ are zero.

Remember

Every matrix factors as A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤ — orthogonal UUU (m×mm\times mm×m), diagonal Σ\SigmaΣ (m×nm\times nm×n, entries σ1≥⋯≥0\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge0σ1​≥⋯≥0), orthogonal VVV (n×nn\times nn×n) — and column by column this says Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​.

#4. Computing the SVD

🧩Background you needtwo facts used below: Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I and "the eigen-decomposition of a symmetric matrix"
  • Orthogonal matrices cancel. If VVV is orthogonal, V⊤V=IV^\top V=IV⊤V=I, so in a product like VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤V\Sigma^\top U^\top U\Sigma V^\topVΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤ the middle U⊤UU^\top UU⊤U simply disappears.
  • Spectral theorem (L06). A symmetric matrix GGG can be written G=QΛQ⊤G=Q\Lambda Q^\topG=QΛQ⊤ with orthonormal eigenvectors in QQQ and eigenvalues on the diagonal of Λ\LambdaΛ. So whenever you manage to write a symmetric matrix as (orthogonal)(diagonal)(same orthogonal)⊤^\top⊤, you have found its eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

Left singular vectors (slide p12). Define G=AA⊤∈Rm×mG=AA^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}G=AA⊤∈Rm×m. Substituting A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤,
G=AA⊤=UΣV⊤ (UΣV⊤)⊤=UΣV⊤VΣ⊤U⊤=U (ΣΣ⊤) U⊤.G=AA^\top=U\Sigma V^\top\,(U\Sigma V^\top)^\top=U\Sigma V^\top V\Sigma^\top U^\top=U\,(\Sigma\Sigma^\top)\,U^\top .G=AA⊤=UΣV⊤(UΣV⊤)⊤=UΣV⊤VΣ⊤U⊤=U(ΣΣ⊤)U⊤.
GGG is symmetric by definition and PSD (§2). ΣΣ⊤\Sigma\Sigma^\topΣΣ⊤ is an m×mm\times mm×m diagonal matrix. So this is an eigen-decomposition of GGG: the columns of UUU are eigenvectors of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤, and its eigenvalues are λ=σ2\lambda=\sigma^2λ=σ2. Since GGG is PSD, λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0. The eigen-decomposition of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ gives the mmm left singular vectors of AAA and the first mmm singular values.

Right singular vectors (slide p13). Define G=A⊤A∈Rn×nG=A^\top A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}G=A⊤A∈Rn×n:
G=A⊤A=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=V (Σ⊤Σ) V⊤.G=A^\top A=V\Sigma^\top U^\top U\Sigma V^\top=V\,(\Sigma^\top\Sigma)\,V^\top .G=A⊤A=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=V(Σ⊤Σ)V⊤.
Σ⊤Σ\Sigma^\top\SigmaΣ⊤Σ is an n×nn\times nn×n diagonal matrix, so the columns of VVV are eigenvectors of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A with eigenvalues λ=σ2≥0\lambda=\sigma^2\ge0λ=σ2≥0. The eigen-decomposition of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A gives the nnn right singular vectors of AAA and the first nnn singular values.

Theorem / Key result: Singular values from eigenvalues

σi=λi(A⊤A)=λi(AA⊤)  (for the non-zero ones),\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^\top A)}=\sqrt{\lambda_i(AA^\top)}\ \ (\text{for the non-zero ones}),σi​=λi​(A⊤A)​=λi​(AA⊤)​  (for the non-zero ones),
and they are never negative, because A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is PSD — "now you can explain the non-negativity of the singular values". A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ have the same non-zero eigenvalues (if A⊤Av=λvA^\top Av=\lambda vA⊤Av=λv then AA⊤(Av)=λ(Av)AA^\top(Av)=\lambda(Av)AA⊤(Av)=λ(Av)); the larger one just has extra zeros.

SVD summary (slide p14). EVD of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ gives UUU and the first mmm singular values; EVD of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A gives VVV and the first nnn singular values; UUU and VVV are always orthogonal; the SVD always exists; the singular values are non-negative.

🔍Where does this come from?why σ1=max⁡∥x∥=1∥Ax∥\sigma_1=\max_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|σ1​=max∥x∥=1​∥Ax∥ — the singular values are the stretch factors

Write a unit vector in the eigenvector basis of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A: x=∑icivix=\sum_ic_iv_ix=∑i​ci​vi​ with ∑ici2=1\sum_ic_i^2=1∑i​ci2​=1. Then
∥Ax∥2=x⊤A⊤Ax=∑iλici2,\|Ax\|^2=x^\top A^\top Ax=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^2 ,∥Ax∥2=x⊤A⊤Ax=i∑​λi​ci2​,
a weighted average of the eigenvalues (the weights ci2c_i^2ci2​ are non-negative and sum to 1). An average cannot exceed the largest value, so ∥Ax∥2≤λ1\|Ax\|^2\le\lambda_1∥Ax∥2≤λ1​, with equality at x=v1x=v_1x=v1​. Hence the largest stretch of a unit vector is λ1=σ1\sqrt{\lambda_1}=\sigma_1λ1​​=σ1​, achieved along v1v_1v1​; the best direction perpendicular to v1v_1v1​ is v2v_2v2​, with stretch σ2\sigma_2σ2​, and so on.

#The recipe — and the sign trap

Definition: Computing an SVD by hand
  1. Form A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and find its eigenvalues λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge0λ1​≥λ2​≥⋯≥0. Then σi=λi\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}σi​=λi​​.
  2. Find unit eigenvectors viv_ivi​ of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A: these are the columns of VVV.
  3. For each σi>0\sigma_i>0σi​>0, set
    ui=Aviσi.u_i=\frac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}.ui​=σi​Avi​​.
  4. If m>rm>rm>r (more output dimensions than non-zero singular values), complete UUU with unit vectors perpendicular to u1,…,uru_1,\dots,u_ru1​,…,ur​; they solve A⊤w=0A^\top w=\mathbf 0A⊤w=0.

Checks: ∑iσi2=∥A∥F2\sum_i\sigma_i^2=\|A\|_F^2∑i​σi2​=∥A∥F2​ (the sum of the squares of all entries); for square AAA, σ1⋯σn=∣det⁡A∣\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n=|\det A|σ1​⋯σn​=∣detA∣.

Common trap: Do not take UUU from a separate eigen-decomposition of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤

Each eigenvector is defined only up to sign, and only one pairing of uiu_iui​ with viv_ivi​ satisfies Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​. If you compute UUU and VVV independently, a sign can come out wrong and UΣV⊤≠AU\Sigma V^\top\ne AUΣV⊤=A. Always get VVV from A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and then define ui=Avi/σiu_i=Av_i/\sigma_iui​=Avi​/σi​. (These uiu_iui​ are automatically perpendicular: ui⊤uj=vi⊤A⊤Avjσiσj=λj vi⊤vjσiσj=0u_i^\top u_j=\dfrac{v_i^\top A^\top Av_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}=\dfrac{\lambda_j\,v_i^\top v_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}=0ui⊤​uj​=σi​σj​vi⊤​A⊤Avj​​=σi​σj​λj​vi⊤​vj​​=0 for i≠ji\neq ji=j.)

Compute an SVD as: eigenvalues of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A give σi=λi\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}σi​=λi​​, its unit eigenvectors give VVV, and ui=Avi/σiu_i=Av_i/\sigma_iui​=Avi​/σi​ gives UUU — never take UUU and VVV from two separate eigen-decompositions.

#5. Geometric interpretation: rotate, stretch, rotate

Read Ax=UΣV⊤xAx=U\Sigma V^\top xAx=UΣV⊤x from right to left (slide p15):

  1. V⊤V^\topV⊤ — transformation (change of basis) in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn. It re-describes xxx using the perpendicular directions v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ as axes; for a picture, it rotates (or reflects) the input. Lengths and angles do not change.
  2. Σ\SigmaΣ — scaling in the new basis. It stretches the iii-th axis by σi\sigma_iσi​, and changes the dimension from nnn to mmm:
    • if m<nm<nm<n, drop the last n−mn-mn−m coordinates (the zero columns of Σ\SigmaΣ);
    • if m>nm>nm>n, append m−nm-nm−n zero coordinates (the zero rows of Σ\SigmaΣ).
  3. UUU — transformation (change of basis) in Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm. It rotates the result onto the output directions u1,…,umu_1,\dots,u_mu1​,…,um​.
Theorem / Key result: Circles become ellipses

The image of the unit circle (ball) under AAA is an ellipse (ellipsoid) whose semi-axes are σ1u1, σ2u2, …, σrur\sigma_1u_1,\ \sigma_2u_2,\ \dots,\ \sigma_ru_rσ1​u1​, σ2​u2​, …, σr​ur​: the lengths of the axes are the singular values, their directions are the left singular vectors, and σ1\sigma_1σ1​ is the largest stretch AAA can produce.

Why. A unit vector x=∑icivix=\sum_ic_iv_ix=∑i​ci​vi​ (with ∑ici2=1\sum_ic_i^2=1∑i​ci2​=1) is sent to Ax=∑iσiciuiAx=\sum_i\sigma_ic_iu_iAx=∑i​σi​ci​ui​. The uiu_iui​ are perpendicular, so the coordinate along uiu_iui​ is σici\sigma_ic_iσi​ci​, which reaches at most σi\sigma_iσi​ (when x=vix=v_ix=vi​).

For BBB (§4): V⊤V^\topV⊤ is a rotation by −45∘-45^\circ−45∘, Σ\SigmaΣ stretches the axes by 35≈6.713\sqrt5\approx6.7135​≈6.71 and 5≈2.24\sqrt5\approx2.245​≈2.24, and UUU is a rotation by +71.6∘+71.6^\circ+71.6∘. The ellipse has area πσ1σ2=15π\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2=15\piπσ1​σ2​=15π, so BBB multiplies areas by 15=∣det⁡B∣15=|\det B|15=∣detB∣.

For the filter (slide p17): the unit circle on the canvas becomes an ellipse with semi-axes 1.62 u11.62\,u_11.62u1​ and 1.0 u21.0\,u_21.0u2​, both lying in the sheet y3=y1+0.8y2y_3=y_1+0.8y_2y3​=y1​+0.8y2​. The third direction u3u_3u3​ is perpendicular to the sheet and never reached — this is the extra zero row of Σ\SigmaΣ ("append 1 more basis"). After stretching, the picture sits in a plane inside R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, and UUU rotates that plane onto the sheet.

#What the matrix reaches, and what it destroys

If rrr singular values are non-zero:

  • u1,…,uru_1,\dots,u_ru1​,…,ur​ span the column space C(A)⊆Rm\mathcal C(A)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^mC(A)⊆Rm (dimension rrr): all outputs that can occur;
  • vr+1,…,vnv_{r+1},\dots,v_nvr+1​,…,vn​ span the null space N(A)⊆Rn\mathcal N(A)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^nN(A)⊆Rn (dimension n−rn-rn−r): a zero singular value squashes that direction to 0\mathbf 00;
  • ur+1,…,umu_{r+1},\dots,u_mur+1​,…,um​ are never reached; they span N(A⊤)\mathcal N(A^\top)N(A⊤).

Its "ellipse" has zero width: the unit circle is flattened onto a segment along u1u_1u1​, from −σ1u1-\sigma_1u_1−σ1​u1​ to σ1u1\sigma_1u_1σ1​u1​, of length 2σ1=65≈13.42\sigma_1=6\sqrt5\approx13.42σ1​=65​≈13.4. The direction v2=15(−2,1)v_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(-2,1)v2​=5​1​(−2,1) is lost for good — no matrix can undo the flattening.

Remember

Every linear map rotates (V⊤V^\topV⊤), stretches along perpendicular axes (Σ\SigmaΣ, dropping or appending coordinates), and rotates again (UUU): the unit circle becomes an ellipse with semi-axes σiui\sigma_iu_iσi​ui​.

#6. Rank and rank estimation

Theorem / Key result: Rank from singular values

The rank of a matrix equals the number of non-zero singular values.

The slide's reason. A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AAA have the same rank (L03: N(A⊤A)=N(A)\mathcal N(A^\top A)=\mathcal N(A)N(A⊤A)=N(A)), and the rank of a symmetric square matrix equals its number of non-zero eigenvalues; those eigenvalues are the σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​.

🔍Where does this come from?a second proof, straight from A=UΣV⊤A=U\Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤

UUU and V⊤V^\topV⊤ are invertible (rotations lose no information), and multiplying by an invertible matrix does not change the rank. So rank⁡A=rank⁡Σ\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}\SigmarankA=rankΣ, and the rank of a diagonal matrix is the number of its non-zero diagonal entries.

Caution (revision notes): "rank = number of non-zero eigenvalues" is true for symmetric matrices such as A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A, but not for every square matrix: [0100]\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}[00​10​] has rank 1 and both eigenvalues 0. Its singular values are 111 and 000 — one non-zero, matching the rank.

#Application: estimating the rank of noisy data (slide p18)

Suppose we have nnn data points a1,…,an∈Rma_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}^ma1​,…,an​∈Rm with n≫mn\gg mn≫m, stacked as the columns of A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n. If the points satisfy some linear relations — they all lie in an rrr-dimensional subspace of Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm — then AAA has rank rrr. But measured data carry errors, so AAA will probably have full rank mmm. Still, only rrr of the singular values will be large; the others will be close to zero (as small as the noise). Using the SVD, we estimate an approximate rank by counting the singular values that are much larger than the others.

Worked example: Eight noisy points near a plane (revision notes, Example 5)

Eight points in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 lie on the plane y3=y1+y2y_3=y_1+y_2y3​=y1​+y2​ (true rank 2), but each entry carries noise of size about 0.050.050.05. The singular values of the 3×83\times83×8 data matrix are
σ1≈5.83,σ2≈2.20,σ3≈0.15.\sigma_1\approx5.83,\qquad \sigma_2\approx2.20,\qquad \sigma_3\approx0.15 .σ1​≈5.83,σ2​≈2.20,σ3​≈0.15.
Two large and one tiny: approximate rank 2, without being told about the plane. The direction u3≈(−0.60,−0.54,0.59)u_3\approx(-0.60,-0.54,0.59)u3​≈(−0.60,−0.54,0.59) is almost the normal 13(−1,−1,1)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1,-1,1)3​1​(−1,−1,1) of the true plane — the direction in which the data barely vary. There is no universal cutoff: look for a clear gap (2.20→0.152.20\to0.152.20→0.15), since with noise no singular value is exactly zero.

Check yourself: a 4×1004\times1004×100 data matrix with singular values 10, 9.5, 0.01, 0.00810,\ 9.5,\ 0.01,\ 0.00810, 9.5, 0.01, 0.008 has approximate rank 2.

Remember

rank AAA = the number of non-zero singular values; with noisy data, count the singular values above the clear gap to get the approximate rank.

#7. Matrix approximation

A matrix as a sum of layers (slide p19). Using the SVD,
A=UΣV⊤=∑i=1min⁡(m,n)ui σi vi⊤.A=U\Sigma V^\top=\sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,n)}u_i\,\sigma_i\,v_i^\top .A=UΣV⊤=i=1∑min(m,n)​ui​σi​vi⊤​.
If rank⁡A=r≤min⁡(m,n)\operatorname{rank}A=r\le\min(m,n)rankA=r≤min(m,n), the summation can be truncated at rrr with no loss: A=∑i=1ruiσivi⊤A=\sum_{i=1}^ru_i\sigma_iv_i^\topA=∑i=1r​ui​σi​vi⊤​. Each layer uivi⊤u_iv_i^\topui​vi⊤​ is an m×nm\times nm×n matrix of rank one (a column times a row), with strength σi\sigma_iσi​; the first layer is the strongest and each later layer adds a finer correction — like a photograph built up from a coarse outline.

Definition: The k-rank approximation

Keeping only the first kkk singular vectors and singular values,
A≈Ak=∑i=1kui σi vi⊤,rank⁡Ak=k.A\approx A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}u_i\,\sigma_i\,v_i^\top,\qquad \operatorname{rank}A_k=k .A≈Ak​=i=1∑k​ui​σi​vi⊤​,rankAk​=k.

How good is it? The error A−Ak=∑i>kσiuivi⊤A-A_k=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^\topA−Ak​=∑i>k​σi​ui​vi⊤​ is the sum of the discarded layers, so:

  • the largest stretch of the error matrix is σk+1\sigma_{k+1}σk+1​;
  • the total squared error is
    ∥A−Ak∥F2=σk+12+σk+22+⋯+σr2;\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sigma_{k+1}^2+\sigma_{k+2}^2+\cdots+\sigma_r^2 ;∥A−Ak​∥F2​=σk+12​+σk+22​+⋯+σr2​;
  • the fraction of the "energy" kept is ∑i≤kσi2∑iσi2\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i^2}{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}∑i​σi2​∑i≤k​σi2​​.

By the Eckart–Young theorem (used without proof), no other rank-kkk matrix does better. (2025 Mid MCQ 22: AkA_kAk​ minimises ∥A−Ak∥F\|A-A_k\|_F∥A−Ak​∥F​ and ∥A−Ak∥F2=∑i>kσi2\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2∥A−Ak​∥F2​=∑i>k​σi2​ — both true; keeping more components never increases the error.)

📄 Original question2025 Mid Part I · MCQ 22 ↗tap to show

The best rank-kkk approximation of AAA is given by (Eckart–Young): (a) Ak=∑i=1kσiuivi⊤A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_iu_iv_i^\topAk​=∑i=1k​σi​ui​vi⊤​ minimises ∥A−Ak∥F\|A-A_k\|_F∥A−Ak​∥F​ (b) ∥A−Ak∥F2=∑i>kσi2\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2∥A−Ak​∥F2​=∑i>k​σi2​ (c) using the smaller singular directions preserves the matrix information in the approximation (d) keeping more components always increases the reconstruction error

A−Ak=U Σrest V⊤A-A_k=U\,\Sigma_{\text{rest}}\,V^\topA−Ak​=UΣrest​V⊤, where Σrest\Sigma_{\text{rest}}Σrest​ is Σ\SigmaΣ with the first kkk diagonal entries set to zero. With k=0k=0k=0 this also gives ∥A∥F2=∑iσi2\|A\|_F^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2∥A∥F2​=∑i​σi2​.

Geometry. Dropping the layer σ2u2v2⊤\sigma_2u_2v_2^\topσ2​u2​v2⊤​ removes the short axis of the ellipse: A1A_1A1​ sends the circle to the segment along the long axis. What is lost is the half-width σ2\sigma_2σ2​; the thinner the ellipse already is, the better a line approximates it.

Worked example: Problem Set 7, Problem 4 — singular values 10, 2, 0.510,\ 2,\ 0.510, 2, 0.5
📄 Original questionPSet 7 · Problem 4 ↗

A data matrix has singular values 101010, 222 and 0.50.50.5. (a) What is its rank? (b) If we keep only the largest singular value, what rank approximation do we obtain, and what is the Frobenius norm of the discarded part? (c) What fraction of the squared Frobenius norm does this rank-one approximation retain?

Worked solution

(a) All three are non-zero, so the rank is 3.
(b) Keeping σ1=10\sigma_1=10σ1​=10 gives a rank-one approximation; the discarded part has
∥A−A1∥F=22+0.52=4.25=172≈2.06.\|A-A_1\|_F=\sqrt{2^2+0.5^2}=\sqrt{4.25}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}\approx2.06 .∥A−A1​∥F​=22+0.52​=4.25​=217​​≈2.06.
(c) Retained fraction =102102+22+0.52=100104.25=400417≈0.959=\dfrac{10^2}{10^2+2^2+0.5^2}=\dfrac{100}{104.25}=\dfrac{400}{417}\approx0.959=102+22+0.52102​=104.25100​=417400​≈0.959, about 95.9%.

#Why it matters: compression

An m×nm\times nm×n matrix stores mnmnmn numbers. AkA_kAk​ needs only kkk vectors ui∈Rmu_i\in\mathbb{R}^mui​∈Rm, kkk numbers σi\sigma_iσi​ and kkk vectors vi∈Rnv_i\in\mathbb{R}^nvi​∈Rn:
storage(Ak)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).\text{storage}(A_k)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).storage(Ak​)=mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).
Images are approximately low rank — their singular values fall off quickly — so a small kkk keeps almost all of the energy. Choosing kkk is the same decision as estimating the approximate rank: look for where the singular values drop.

Worked example: Problem Set 7, Problem 9 — image compression
📄 Original questionPSet 7 · Problem 9 ↗

An image is a matrix A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n of pixel intensities with rank-kkk SVD approximation Ak=UkΣkVk⊤A_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^\topAk​=Uk​Σk​Vk⊤​. (a) How many real numbers are needed to store AAA directly, and to store the three factors of AkA_kAk​? (b) Compare these for a 1000×8001000\times8001000×800 image with k=20k=20k=20. (c) Explain why increasing kkk improves fidelity but reduces compression.

Worked solution

(a) Directly: mnmnmn. Factors: mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1)mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1)mk+k+kn=k(m+n+1).
(b) 1000×800=800,0001000\times800=800{,}0001000×800=800,000 values directly; with k=20k=20k=20, 20(1000+800+1)=36,02020(1000+800+1)=36{,}02020(1000+800+1)=36,020 values, about 4.5%.
(c) Adding components can only reduce (or keep) the best rank-kkk error, so more detail is preserved; but each extra component costs m+n+1m+n+1m+n+1 more numbers, so the saving shrinks.

The same count in the mids: 2025 Mid P1 (2048×15362048\times15362048×1536, k=80k=80k=80: 286,800286{,}800286,800 instead of 3,145,7283{,}145{,}7283,145,728, a 90.88% saving) and 2024 Mid P1 (1920×10801920\times10801920×1080, k=120k=120k=120: 360,120360{,}120360,120 instead of 2,073,6002{,}073{,}6002,073,600).

Ak=∑i≤kσiuivi⊤A_k=\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^\topAk​=∑i≤k​σi​ui​vi⊤​ is the best rank-kkk approximation; its squared error is ∑i>kσi2\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2∑i>k​σi2​ and it costs k(m+n+1)k(m+n+1)k(m+n+1) numbers to store.
